transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman, Iran's Supreme Leader met with Iranian
military officials over the weekend.
This was to deliver directives for a potential return of hostilities with the U.S. and Israel.
That is according to Iranian state media.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shelchi reports this comes during a flurry of diplomatic visits in the
minis trying to stave off a war.
On Saturday, Iranian state media reported that Ayatollah Mushtaba Khamenei said that
any kind of threat to Iran would face a "immediate and impactful response."
The spokesperson for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps also said Sunday that there will
be "no geographical limitations" during a possible war and that new U.S. and Israeli
targets have been identified.
He did not provide details on what they were.
Meanwhile, during a Saturday interview with Al Jazeera, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas
Arakji said that Iran had reached a new proposal with mediators to reopen the Strait of Hormuz
in two days, but did not expand on what the plan involved.
Hadil Al-Shelchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
Dozens of supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber attack the second
time in less than a month.
NPR's Rebecca Rossman reports hackers allegedly targeted refrigeration systems forcing stores
to throw away food.
Supermarkets in at least six European countries were affected, including Sweden, Belgium,
Luxembourg, Ireland, and the Netherlands.
Several stores reported temperatures inside their fridges and freezers reaching 122 degrees
Fahrenheit.
One supermarket chain in Belgium said it lost over $100,000 worth of produce.
It's unclear who is behind the latest attacks, which come just weeks after similar attacks
hit more than 400 supermarkets across France.
Paris' national cybersecurity agency says hackers took control of refrigeration controllers
supplied by a Danish company, costing supermarkets tens of millions of dollars in spoiled food.
Rebecca Rossman, NPR News, Paris.
The latest NPR/PBS News Marist poll finds 37 percent of likely voters have a favorable
impression of President Trump.
Meanwhile, 58 percent have a negative one.
Member Station WHYY Carmen Russell Sluchansky reports on two Pennsylvania Republican incumbents
who are treating the president very differently.
Republican U.S. Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Bucks County is campaigning on his appeal
as a moderate.
I'm ranked number one most independent on every scorecard, every single metric.
Halfway across the state, Representative Scott Perry of Cumberland County continues to publicly
applaud President Trump.
Here he is talking to Newsmax.
A lot of great things are happening in the world.
We've won both of these swing districts in 2024, but Democrats believe they can flip
them this election.
Recent polling and campaign finance reports suggest they have a better shot at Perry.
For NPR News, I'm Carmen Russell Sluchansky in Bucks County.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Doctors for Connecticut Democratic Senator Chris Murphy say he had a stroke Saturday.
They say Murphy has been awake and alert, and they expect him to make a full recovery.
In Los Angeles, the retrial begins for the man accused of starting a fire that eventually
turned into the deadly 2025 Palisades fire, Steve Futterman reports.
The prosecution claims Jonathan Rinderknecht was angry and despondent when he allegedly
started the Lockman fire in the early hours of January 1st last year.
That fire, the prosecution says, smoldered for around a week before reigniting later
as the Palisades fire.
The defense has a much different view.
It says the Lockman fire was likely ignited by New Year's fireworks.
Former federal prosecutor Lori Levinson says in the original trial jurors nearly found
Rinderknecht not guilty.
The jury hung, leaning 10 to 2 for acquittal.
So the government does have an uphill battle.
The defense says prosecutors are simply looking for a scapegoat.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman in Los Angeles.
After our flood watches and warnings up in the Four Corners area today, heavy storms
poured a lot of rain on parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah.
It flooded rivers and triggered evacuations.
The National Weather Service says the storms are triggered by an atmospheric river from
the Pacific.
Meanwhile officials in India are evacuating people away from the coast ahead of a second
cyclone in a week's time.
I'm Cora Vekulman, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Iran's Supreme Leader meets military officials to deliver directives amid fears of renewed hostilities with U.S. and Israel
Iran's foreign minister says a new proposal with mediators would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days
Cyberattack hits dozens of European supermarkets, spoiling food by disabling refrigeration systems in at least six countries
NPR/PBS Marist poll finds 37 percent of likely voters view President Trump favorably, 58 percent unfavorably
Pennsylvania Republicans Brian Fitzpatrick and Scott Perry take sharply different approaches to backing President Trump in 2026 races
Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy suffers a stroke; doctors expect full recovery
Retrial begins in Los Angeles for Jonathan Rinderknecht, accused of starting the fire that became the 2025 Palisades fire
Heavy storms and atmospheric river cause flooding and evacuations across Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah
India evacuates coastal residents ahead of a second cyclone within a week
